name: Rue des Francs-Bourgeois
short_description: 14th-century Marais shopping street whose name derives from a 1415 alms-house for tax-exempt poor 'francs-bourgeois' donated by the philanthropist Mazurier.

_pipeline.address: Rue des Francs-Bourgeois, 75003/75004 Paris (runs between Rue des Archives and Place des Vosges)
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Marais's premier shopping spine and one of the few Paris streets that historically opens on Sundays; lined with hôtels particuliers including Carnavalet and Lamoignon.

name: Hôtel de Chenizot
short_description: 1719 Île Saint-Louis mansion remodeled by Pierre Vigné de Vigny, where Archbishop Affre died in 1848 after being shot at a June Days barricade.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Classed historic monument with celebrated rocaille balcony; home to Madame Tallien before the Revolution and to metaphysician René Guénon 1904–1930.

name: Pont de la Tournelle
short_description: 1928 stone bridge linking Île Saint-Louis to the Left Bank, crowned by Paul Landowski's 14-metre statue of Saint Geneviève protecting a child Paris.

_pipeline.address: Pont de la Tournelle, between Quai d'Orléans (Île Saint-Louis) and Quai de la Tournelle, 75005 Paris
discovery_sources: Un Jour de Plus à Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Named for a tower of the Philippe-Auguste wall; replaced by current span after the 1910 flood. Landowski sulked at the inauguration because the statue did not face Notre-Dame.

name: Rue Lepic
short_description: Winding Montmartre street where Vincent and Theo van Gogh shared a third-floor flat at no. 54 from 1886 to 1888 and where Café des Deux Moulins doubled as Amélie's workplace at no. 15.

_pipeline.address: Rue Lepic, 75018 Paris (runs from Boulevard de Clichy to Place Jean-Baptiste-Clément)
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Renamed in 1864 for General Louis Lepic; site of Louis Renault's 1898 Voiturette hill-climb wager and home to two surviving Montmartre windmills.

name: Maison Loo
short_description: Ochre-red Chinese pagoda built in 1926 by dealer C.T. Loo from a Haussmann-era townhouse, now Europe's first Asian-art gallery and a private events venue.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Architect Fernand Bloch transformed the building for collector Ching Tsai Loo in 1925–26; classed monument historique in 2002/2006 for its 18th-century lacquer-panel salons.

name: Hôtel Menier
short_description: Second-Empire rotunda mansion built 1869–74 by Henri Parent for chocolate magnate Émile-Justin Menier and credited as Zola's model for the private hôtel in La Curée.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Sculpted façade attributed to Jules Dalou faces Parc Monceau; the Menier 'M' monogram is still visible on the rotunda. Now subdivided into private apartments.

name: Église de la Sainte-Trinité
short_description: Neo-Renaissance Second-Empire church (1861–67) by Théodore Ballu with a 65-metre belfry, where Olivier Messiaen served as organist for 61 years until 1992.

_pipeline.address: 3 rue de la Trinité (Place d'Estienne d'Orves), 75009 Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Built as part of Haussmann's Chaussée d'Antin renewal; served as a hospital during the 1870 Siege of Paris.

name: InterContinental Paris Le Grand
short_description: Five-star hotel inaugurated by Empress Eugénie in 1862 facing the Palais Garnier, financed by the Pereire brothers ahead of the 1867 Universal Exhibition.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Houses the Salon Opéra ballroom under a 14-metre glass canopy; the rue Scribe entrance has been the main door since 1905.

name: Impasse Sandrié
short_description: Short cul-de-sac opened in 1775 on land leased by the Mathurins to Jérôme Sandrié, today housing a former Calmann-Lévy printing works structured by Gustave Eiffel.

_pipeline.address: Impasse Sandrié, 75009 Paris (between Place Charles-Garnier and Square de l'Opéra-Louis-Jouvet)
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Hidden alley a few steps from the Palais Garnier; preserves a glass-roofed 19th-century printing house with monumental bookcases.

name: Passerelle Léopold-Sédar-Senghor
short_description: 106-metre single-arch footbridge in tropical ipê wood by Marc Mimram (1997–99), renamed in 2006 for the Senegalese poet on the centenary of his birth.

_pipeline.address: Passerelle Léopold-Sédar-Senghor, between Quai des Tuileries (75001) and Quai Anatole-France (75007), Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Replaces a Napoleon-III cast-iron span (1861) demolished in 1961; won Mimram the 1999 Prix de l'Équerre d'Argent.

name: Bourse de Commerce — Pinault Collection
short_description: François Pinault's contemporary-art museum opened in 2021 inside a circular former corn exchange, with a concrete cylinder inserted under the cast-iron dome by Tadao Ando.
name_variations: La Bourse du Commerce — Pinault Collection

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Houses the Médicis astronomical column at its flank; 6,800 m² of galleries spanning a 16th-century site that became the world's first cast-iron-domed market.

name: Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel
short_description: Neoclassical triumphal arch built 1806–08 by Percier and Fontaine, originally topped by the Horses of Saint Mark looted from Venice and returned in 1815.

_pipeline.address: Place du Carrousel, 75001 Paris (between the Louvre and the Tuileries)
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Modeled on the Arch of Septimius Severus; its eight Corinthian marble columns were salvaged from the demolished Château de Meudon.
